sections.heading: ON STUDYING LITERATURE
sections.content:
Q: I actually want to become a novelist myself (I'm currently in high school). I wanted to ask you something: do I really need to major in literature at university if I want to become a novelist?

A: My own university didn't even have a literature department. I think literature departments are places to study literature, not places that teach you how to write novels.[ref:university] Just pick whatever major interests you.

sections.heading: ON PSYCHOLOGY AND EMOTION
sections.content:
Q: I'm studying psychology, and whenever I read your work, I find myself thinking, somewhat rudely, "What perspective does this person use to look at human emotions?"

A: Funny enough, I'm curious about the opposite — what perspective people who study psychology use to look at human emotions.

sections.heading: ON THE TIME-TRAVEL TRICK
sections.content:
Q: I couldn't accept the line "I refuse to answer any questions!" from the afterword of Ashita mo Kare ni Koisuru, so I'm asking anyway.[ref:ashita-mo-kare] In Kinou mo Kare wo Aishiteta, the ones who traveled back "nine years" were Nia (me) and Machi (her) — so who was it that returned to the "original time"? Or rather, was Nia actually Ayano Garasu (me), or was Nia actually Chikao Hayashida? The manga often has scenes where the characters explain the time travel using diagrams on a whiteboard, so I tried mapping out the characters and events that way myself, but I still can't make sense of it. Please, do something about this! I'm just going to force this question on you.

A: I'm sorry, but I can't explain a story I wrote myself... or rather, I don't want to. It would be like explaining my own joke — incredibly awkward. So, sorry.

sections.heading: HOW ARE YOU?
sections.content:
Q: How are you doing?

A: Fine, thank you! And you?

sections.heading: ON BECOMING A PROFESSIONAL WRITER
sections.content:
Q: So, I want to become a professional writer. My father is retiring in six years, and I don't want to keep being a burden to him after that happens. So I'd like to start working while I'm still a student. I want to become someone who does what I love. The problem is, I'm not good at writing. I come up with all kinds of story ideas, but even the ones I manage to actually write turn out badly right away. Could you tell me some techniques or practice methods for writing novels?

A: If you can come up with stories, you're already fine. You don't need techniques or practice — the important thing is just to aim to get the story into some kind of finished shape first. Don't give up. Even if the writing itself is a little rough, as long as the story is interesting, that will make up for it. Just look at my early work — it was pretty terrible.

sections.heading: FAVORITE GAMES
sections.content:
Q: Do you have any games you like?

A: Lots, actually. Lately I've been really into GOD EATER.[ref:god-eater]

sections.heading: A DENPA ONNA GAME?
sections.content:
Q: I read Denpa Onna — it was such a fun novel![ref:denpa-onna] I'm completely hooked on it now. So... I've been thinking it would be great if there were a Denpa Onna game. I really hope you'll consider it!

A: No, honestly, I want that too. But realistically, it's probably not going to happen... sorry.

sections.heading: FAVORITE BOOKS
sections.content:
Q: Do you have any favorite books?

A: There are a lot, but of the ones I've read this year — actually, wait, I haven't read anything this year. My favorite is Otsuichi's The Forgotten Story.[ref:wasurerarenaimonogatari]

sections.heading: UNRESOLVED MYSTERIES
sections.content:
Q: I found myself gradually understanding the trick behind Kinou mo Kare wo Aishiteta and Ashita mo Kare ni Koisuru as I read, but there are still parts that bother me. I'd be really happy if there were ever an official explanation of some kind.

A: Even I have... parts I don't fully understand either.

sections.heading: WORDS FOR A NEW FATHER
sections.content:
Q: I'm a father now. Please give me some words of encouragement.

A: Looking back on my own childhood, just imagining how hard it must be to raise a child already gives me a headache. It's a pretty ordinary thing to say, but please keep at it. I respect you for it.

sections.heading: ON A HARD-TO-FIND SERIAL
sections.content:
Q: I heard that the continuation of Chotto Muteki, Daitai Kodomo can only be read on mobile platforms like i-mode's "i-land."[ref:chotto-muteki] Since I don't have a mobile phone, I can't read it. Is there any chance of being able to read it on a computer?

A: There are plans to add extra material and release it as a paperback, so please look forward to that.

sections.heading: A LIFE STORY, IN BRIEF
sections.content:
Q: Please tell me, in as much detail as possible, how your life has been up until now.

A: I haven't really done anything worth describing in detail... nothing especially unique. I used to be a kid who loved manga, hated reading novels, and loved video games more than anything. Honestly, not much has changed since then.

sections.heading: ADVICE FOR A FIRST-TIME WRITER
sections.content:
Q: I'm a freelancer with nothing in particular I want to do, just drifting through each day without much meaning to it. But after reading your books, I started wanting to write something like your work — I started wanting to become a novelist myself. With that in mind, I'm currently writing a novel in my own way. I found a subject I think is interesting and started writing it, but since I have zero experience, it's coming out badly, and it's been frustrating. How did you first start writing? If possible, I'd love some advice.

A: At first, I just wrote down scenes I thought of, scenes I wanted to write, with no real structure to them. Then, in order to connect the story to those scenes, I started filling in the parts in between — that's roughly how I ended up with a finished story. I wouldn't worry too much about whether something is "well-written" or "badly-written." There's a thing people call writing ability, but there's no actual device in the world that can measure it. If you've got a subject you find interesting, just go for it.

sections.heading: MOTIVATION, COURAGE, AND POINKIKKI
sections.content:
Q: Motivation, courage, and Poinkikki — which of these does a writer need?[ref:poinkikki]

A: Keep your motivation at "good" or above at all times! That's what the strategy guide for Power Pro says.[ref:power-pro]

sections.heading: ON TAKING AN APPRENTICE
sections.content:
Q: How do you learn to write like that? I want to write light novels. I write every day, but I just can't seem to grasp how to come up with unique stories or clever phrasing. I want to become a professional writer. Actually, why don't you just take me on as your apprentice?

A: If you want to become a professional writer, go to a novel-writing school... but seriously, since I have no idea how to actually teach someone, I don't take on apprentices. If you want to become a professional, the important thing is just to write — writing is the only way to improve. Even in my own case, there's a world of difference between the writing in my debut work and the writing in my most recent one. Also, this isn't really related, but I'd personally avoid enrolling in any school that specifically brands itself as a "novel-writing" institution.

sections.heading: A RIVAL'S REQUEST
sections.content:
Q: Please let me be your rival.

A: What?!

sections.heading: THE ULTIMATE GOAL
sections.content:
Q: Please tell me your ultimate goal as a writer.

A: Win some kind of award, I guess. Also, become number one in the world. Honestly, that's still my favorite goal.

sections.heading: A SEQUEL TO HANASAKI TAROU?
sections.content:
Q: Also, I wanted to ask — is there ever going to be a sequel to Hanasaki Tarou?[ref:hanasaki-tarou] I'm not really expecting an answer just by asking here, but I really love the Hanasaki Tarou series (though I'm not sure two books counts as a "series")... it would be great if it could continue.

A: If it sells just a little more...

sections.heading: A FAVORITE CHARACTER
sections.content:
Q: Who's your favorite character among the ones you've created yourself?

A: I don't really have one like that. I don't have a least favorite either.

sections.heading: ON STUDYING NOVEL WRITING
sections.content:
Q: Did you study novel writing in university?

A: I didn't study it formally, but I spent the whole time writing in a notebook during class.

sections.heading: A REQUEST FOR A YUKATA
sections.content:
Q: Please give me a yukata!

A: Why?! Why on earth?! My build is pointlessly large, so there's a good chance the size wouldn't even fit you.[ref:yukata]

sections.heading: ON ENDINGS
sections.content:
Q: I really like the characters, the plot developments, and the "settings" in your novels, but there are also parts I can't quite accept... how should I put this — I'm still pretty childish myself, and I can't really expect to grow out of it anytime soon, so I want clean, tidy endings. A lot of people seem to find endings that leave lingering questions appealing, in a sort of itch-you-can't-scratch way, but I'm not one of those people. Take Ashita mo Kare ni Koisuru, for example — no matter what, I can't accept an ending along the lines of "and the battle continues on" (a phrase commonly associated with stories that get cut short). What I'm trying to say is, whether it's a happy ending or a bad one, I want to see an ending that wraps up absolutely everything about the story. So, um, how should I put this — if it's at all possible, could you write something along the lines of "and here, the story ends completely"? No, it's fine if you ignore this request entirely, but there's a small, hopeful part of me that will keep dreaming, just in case you do write something like that.

A: Hmm — the request is a little too abstract for me to fully grasp, but Tokage Ou might end up with an ending that doesn't lead into anything further.[ref:tokage-ou] And the book coming out in November from MediaWorks Bunko — that one will be a complete single volume, so hopefully that works for you.[ref:yuiitsu-no-negai]

sections.heading: ON THE LIVE-ACTION FILM
sections.content:
Q: I watched the live-action movie! If you became the director yourself, what kind of movie would you make?[ref:live-action-film]

A: I'd want to make something like the game Machi.[ref:machi]

sections.heading: ON N743327
sections.content:
Q: I've been reading the novel on your website — did N743327 end after just four chapters?[ref:n743327] If it doesn't get in the way of your regular work, I'd love it if you could write more whenever you have free time; it would make me really happy. Please keep up the good work going forward too.

A: It's updating irregularly, but I do still plan to keep writing it. For the most part, what gets posted there is more experimental, playful work, so I'd appreciate it if people kept that in mind and took the long view on it.

references.title: Meijo University
references.note: Iruma Hitoma attended Meijo University, which indeed has no literature department, supporting the claim made in his answer.

references.title: Kinou mo Kare wo Aishiteta / Ashita mo Kare ni Koisuru
references.note: The questioner clearly misunderstands the two books being referenced; the exact plot mechanics they're asking about don't align with the actual text. Readers may want to skip this exchange.

references.title: God Eater (2010)
references.source: Video Game by Bandai Namco / Shift
references.note: An action RPG in which players hunt monstrous creatures called Aragami using shapeshifting weapons. Iruma cites it as a game he was into around the time of this Q&A.

references.title: Denpa Onna to Seishun Otoko
references.note: One of Iruma Hitoma's novel series, later adapted into an anime. The questioner is a fan asking about a potential video game adaptation.

references.title: Ushinawareru Monogatari (失はれる物語)
references.note: A short story collection by the acclaimed Japanese horror/mystery author Otsuichi, published by Kadokawa Bunko in 2006, whom Iruma names as a favorite. The title translates more literally as 'A Story That Is Lost' or 'The Story of What Was Lost.'

references.title: Chotto Muteki, Daitai Kodomo
references.note: A novel Iruma began serializing in October 2010 across several Kadokawa-affiliated mobile novel platforms, with the protagonist being Kisogawa as a child. To this day, there has been no sign of it actually being released as a paperback, and since the platforms it was hosted on have since shut down, readers currently have essentially no way to access this work.

references.title: Ponkikki
references.note: A long-running Japanese children's TV show. The questioner included it purely because it rhymed with the other two words in the original Japanese question and has no actual bearing on the answer.

references.title: Power Pro (Jikkyou Powerful Pro Yakyuu)
references.note: A long-running Japanese baseball video game series known for its stat-boosting training mode, which includes a 'motivation' (yaruki) gauge — the source of Iruma's joke.

references.title: Hanasaki Tarou
references.note: A two-book novel series by Iruma Hitoma. The questioner is uncertain whether two entries is enough to call it a proper 'series.'

references.title: Iruma Hitoma's Appearance
references.note: Iruma Hitoma is known for frequently wearing traditional Japanese clothing such as kimono or yukata, and for his notably tall height, which is the basis for his joking concern about sizing.

references.title: Tokage Ou (蜥蜴王)
references.note: Iruma suggests here that this story's ending won't leave loose threads the way the questioner dislikes. In reality, however, the serialization of Tokage Ou was later discontinued and never received an ending at all.

references.title: Yuiitsu no Negai
references.note: The book referenced here as 'the one coming out in November from MediaWorks Bunko.' It was indeed released as a complete, self-contained single volume, matching the kind of decisive ending the questioner had asked for.

references.title: Usotsuki Mii-kun to Kowareta Maa-chan (嘘つきみーくんと壊れたまーちゃん)
references.note: The 2011 live-action film adaptation of Iruma Hitoma's long-running novel series of the same name, referenced by the questioner as the film they had just watched.

references.title: Machi (街 〜運命の交差点〜)
references.note: A live-action sound novel game by Chunsoft told through interwoven storylines and real filmed footage of Shibuya, notable for its multi-perspective, cinematic structure. Iruma cites its style as something he'd want to emulate if directing a film.

references.title: N743327
references.note: One of Iruma Hitoma's serialized works published on his official website. Chapter 1 was posted on October 2, 2011, and Chapter 5 was posted on May 24, 2013, ending with 'to be continued' — but it has never been updated since.
